headline: A claimed proof of the Bochner–Riesz conjecture in three dimensions, in its strict-order form.
scope: The claim is for ℝ³ only, with every order strictly above the conjectured threshold. Endpoint orders are not covered.
plain: Bochner–Riesz means rebuild a function from its frequencies while softening the cut-off at the edge of a ball. The conjecture says how little softening keeps the size of the function under control. This paper claims the three-dimensional case, starting from the hardest exponent, p = 3. There any positive amount of softening is claimed to be enough. Interpolation then gives the full conjectured range.
doesNot: This does not cover endpoint orders, dimensions other than three, or maximal Bochner–Riesz operators.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Salomon Bochner, spherical means for multiple Fourier series
scorecard.significanceWhy: The Bochner–Riesz conjecture in three dimensions is a central open problem in harmonic analysis, and it implies the sphere restriction conjecture.

explanation:
Take a function on three-dimensional space and split it into its frequencies, using the Fourier transform. Keep only frequencies of size below 1, but soften the edge. Multiply each frequency ξ inside the unit ball by (1 − |ξ|²)^δ, and drop those outside. The order δ sets how soft the edge is. With δ = 1, a frequency of size 0.9 keeps 1 − 0.81 = 0.19 of its weight. With δ = 0.1 it keeps 0.19^0.1, about 0.847. At size 0.99 it keeps 0.0199^0.1, about 0.676. So a small δ gives an edge that is almost sharp.

This operation is the Bochner–Riesz mean T_δ. The question is how much softening keeps the function's Lᵖ size under control[13]. The Lᵖ norm is the p-th root of the integral of |f|ᵖ. The conjecture says that δ > max{3|1/p − 1/2| − 1/2, 0} is enough in three dimensions. At p = 3, the first term is 3 × 1/6 − 1/2 = 0, so any δ > 0 should work. At p = 4 the threshold is 3/4 − 1/2 = 1/4. At p = 1 it is 3/2 − 1/2 = 1.

Riesz and Bochner introduced such means to sum Fourier series. In 1971, Fefferman showed that the sharp edge, δ = 0, fails for every p ≠ 2 in two or more dimensions[3]. His proof used a Kakeya construction, a set packed with thin tubes pointing in many directions. Carleson and Sjölin settled the plane in 1972[4]. In three dimensions, Lee reached the conjectured range when max{p, p′} ≥ 10/3[5]. Here p′ is the dual exponent, with 1/p + 1/p′ = 1. Wu lowered the bound to 13/4[6]. Gao, Wu and Xi lowered it to 22/7[7]. Tao showed that the Bochner–Riesz conjecture implies the restriction conjecture for the sphere[8]. Zipeng Wang has also proposed a proof of the conjecture in all dimensions[9].

This paper claims that T_δ is bounded on L³ for every δ > 0[1]. Interpolation and duality then give the full conjectured range[2]. Interpolation fills in exponents between two known bounds, and duality swaps p with p′. The hard case is p = 3, where the conjectured order drops all the way to zero. For 3/2 ≤ p ≤ 3, the paper claims any mild spherical smoothing recovers the function[10].

The key geometric input is the sharp planar Furstenberg estimate of Ren and Wang[11]. A Furstenberg estimate limits how small a set can be when many lines each meet it in a large piece. Another paper in the release reaches the same range by a separate route, through local smoothing for waves[12].

How sure is this? There is no Lean scope note for this result, so no computer proof checker has tested it. The paper is long and depends on the recent Ren–Wang estimate. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Landmark if the proof holds, since it claims a central conjecture in three dimensions. It is one long paper with no Lean scope note. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: The split of a function into frequencies, each with its own strength.
The operation that keeps frequencies inside the unit ball, weighted by (1 − |ξ|²) to the power δ.
The power that sets how softly the frequency cut-off falls to zero at the edge of the ball.
A measure of a function's size: the p-th root of the integral of its absolute value to the power p.
A method that turns bounds at two exponents into bounds at the exponents between them.
A set containing a thin tube, or line segment, in many directions.
A lower bound on the size of a set that many lines each meet in a large piece.
